name: Liraglutide

b.x: A 13% reduction in heart attacks, strokes, and cardiovascular death across 9,340 patients over 3.8 years. That LEADER trial finding [1] made liraglutide the first GLP-1 drug proven to protect the heart. Liraglutide (also sold as Victoza for diabetes and Saxenda for weight management) is a modified version of human GLP-1 with 97% amino acid homology to the native hormone. A palmitic acid chain at position 26 lets it bind albumin in the blood. That binding shields it from DPP-IV breakdown and extends the half-life from about 2 minutes to roughly 13 hours, long enough for once-daily dosing. On the weight side, the SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial (n=3,731) [2] showed 8.0% mean body weight loss at 56 weeks on the 3 mg dose versus 2.6% on placebo. A head-to-head comparison in STEP 8 (PMC8753508) put those numbers in context: semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly produced 15.8% loss versus 6.4% for liraglutide 3 mg daily over 68 weeks. The practical picture for most users looks like this: a pre-filled pen (no mixing needed), weekly dose increases from 0.6 mg up to 3.0 mg, and GI side effects that peak during titration but usually settle within a few weeks. Appetite suppression kicks in within days of the first injection. FDA approved Teva's generic of Saxenda in August 2025.

A C-16 fatty acid (palmitic acid) attached via a glutamic acid spacer at position 26. That single modification gives liraglutide its clinical utility. The palmitic acid promotes non-covalent binding to serum albumin, which does two things: it shields the molecule from DPP-IV and neutral endopeptidase degradation, and it slows absorption from the subcutaneous injection site. Native GLP-1 has a plasma half-life of about 2 minutes. Liraglutide's is roughly 13 hours. Once circulating, liraglutide activates GLP-1 receptors across multiple tissues. In the pancreas, it boosts glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppresses inappropriate glucagon release. The glucose-dependent part is important; hypoglycemia risk stays low when liraglutide is used alone because insulin release only ramps up when blood sugar is raised. In the GI tract, gastric emptying slows by 10 to 15%. In the brain, liraglutide acts on hypothalamic and brainstem GLP-1 receptors to reduce appetite and food reward signaling. The cardiovascular protection spotted in LEADER [1] likely involves direct effects on vascular endothelial function and anti-inflammatory pathways, though the exact mechanisms are still being mapped out.
Liraglutide benefits center on proven weight loss, cardiovascular protection, and a safety profile backed by more than a decade of post-market data.
8.0% mean body weight loss at 56 weeks on 3 mg daily in the SCALE trial (n=3,731) [2]. Real-world results typically land between 5% and 8%.

Cardiovascular protection confirmed in LEADER (n=9,340): 13% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events over 3.8 years of follow-up [1]. That trial was one of the first to prove a diabetes drug could protect the heart.
Short half-life (13 hours) means side effects clear within about a day if you need to pause. Semaglutide's weekly dosing locks you in for seven days if problems arise.
No reconstitution or mixing. Saxenda ships as a pre-filled pen. Dial your dose and inject.
Approved for adolescent obesity (ages 12 and up) since 2020, making it one of the few GLP-1 options with a pediatric indication.
HbA1c reductions of 1.1% to 1.4% at the Victoza dose range (1.2 to 1.8 mg daily), with blood sugar improvements reported even in non-diabetic users.
Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 10 key studies · FDA-approved
FDA-approved for chronic weight management (Saxenda, 3 mg/day) and type 2 diabetes (Victoza, up to 1.8 mg/day).
Dosing studied: 0.6 mg/day (titration start) → 3.0 mg/day (Saxenda maintenance); 1.2–1.8 mg/day (Victoza/T2D)

Strong RCT evidence for ~8% weight loss at 56 weeks and 13% MACE reduction in high-CV-risk T2D. Well-characterized safety profile after 15+ years on market. Less effective than semaglutide or tirzepatide for weight loss.
Key Study

SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes (PMID 26132939): n=3,731, 3 mg/day vs placebo, 56 wk: 8.0% vs 2.6% mean weight loss. LEADER (PMID 27295427): n=9,340 T2D high-CV-risk, 3.8-yr median follow-up: 13% MACE reduction (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.97). STEP 8 head-to-head (PMC8753508): semaglutide 2.4 mg/wk vs liraglutide 3 mg/day, 68 wk: −15.8% vs −6.4% weight loss.
Limitations

Substantially less effective than semaglutide (-6.4% vs -15.8% in STEP 8) and tirzepatide. Daily injection vs once-weekly alternatives. Weight regain expected on discontinuation. Black box warning for medullary thyroid carcinoma (rodent data only; LEADER found 0 MTC in liraglutide arm vs 1 placebo). Slight numerical imbalance in total malignancies in LEADER (10.1% liraglutide vs 9.0% placebo, HR ~1.06, not statistically significant: clinical relevance unclear). Pancreatitis rate similar to placebo in LEADER.
Community Experience
Regarded as the "old reliable" GLP-1: effective, well-understood, and now accessible via generic and compounding.
Community dosing: 0.6 mg/day titration start; most users target 1.2–1.8 mg/day as effective maintenance; some push to 3.0 mg for max effect

Most users follow the FDA titration closely. The daily injection and lower weight loss vs semaglutide drive switching; many transition to semaglutide or tirzepatide after experiencing or researching the options.

Science & Community Aligned

Community closely follows FDA titration protocol. Real-world outcomes (~5–8% weight loss at maintenance) are consistent with trial data. The primary divergence is that many community users elect to stay at sub-maximal doses (1.2–1.8 mg) rather than pushing to 3.0 mg: driven by tolerability, not ignorance of dosing. No significant off-label dose escalation patterns observed.
FDA Label Saxenda FDA Prescribing Information (2026), NDA 206321 (n=3,731 (SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes)) [Source](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/206321Orig1s024lbl.pdf)

Liraglutide comes as a pre-filled pen, so there's no reconstitution math to worry about. Saxenda pens hold 18 mg total and deliver doses from 0.6 mg to 3.0 mg via a dial selector. At the 3 mg maintenance dose, one pen lasts 6 days. For compounded liraglutide from 503A pharmacies, the common concentration is 6 mg/mL. With that concentration in a standard insulin syringe: 10 units equals 0.6 mg, 20 units equals 1.2 mg, 30 units equals 1.8 mg, 40 units equals 2.4 mg, and 50 units equals 3.0 mg. The thing most beginners miss: if you skip more than 3 consecutive days, you need to restart at 0.6 mg and re-titrate. Jumping back to your prior dose after a gap causes disproportionate GI distress. Keep your pens on schedule or plan for the ramp back up. Store unused pens in the fridge (2 to 8 degrees Celsius). Once you start using a pen, it can stay at room temperature (up to 30 degrees Celsius) for 30 days.
Cycling Protocol
Designed for continuous long-term use. Weight regain expected after discontinuation. If you miss more than 3 consecutive days, restart at 0.6mg and re-titrate.
Liraglutide Cycle

Liraglutide is an FDA-approved chronic weight management medication designed for continuous long-term use. Cycling is not recommended: discontinuation results in weight regain. Its listed cycle (52 weeks on, no scheduled off period) reflects this. Users who stop liraglutide and wish to restart after a gap of >3 days should re-titrate from 0.6 mg to minimize GI side effects.
If stopping due to adverse effects: slow taper (step down one dose level per week) to minimize rebound hunger
Weight regain begins within weeks of discontinuation: plan for ongoing therapy or transition to another GLP-1
If stopping for surgery: follow anesthesiologist guidance on GLP-1 washout (typically 1 week minimum due to gastric emptying effects)

Remove the pen from the refrigerator 15 to 30 minutes before injecting. Room-temperature solution reduces injection discomfort.
It should be clear and colorless. Do not use if cloudy or if you see particles.

Community-reported fat-loss pairing: AOD-9604 targets adipose lipolysis via a different mechanism (GH fragment). No clinical interaction data; anecdotal stacking for additional fat mobilization.

Used by community to manage GLP-1-induced GI side effects. BPC-157 is a gut mucosal healing peptide; anecdotally reported to reduce liraglutide-related nausea and GI discomfort. No clinical trial data for this combination.
Cagrilintide

Amylin analog clinically studied in combination with semaglutide (CagriSema) for additive weight loss. With liraglutide, a combined effect is theoretical: complementary mechanism via amylin receptor. No liraglutide-specific combo trial.
Research-stage only; no established human dosing for liraglutide + cagrilintide combination
Avoid
Insulin (any type)

Using liraglutide with insulin may raise the risk of hypoglycemia, including severe hypoglycemia. The Victoza label says to consider a lower insulin dose when starting liraglutide (section 7.2). Saxenda says a lower insulin dose may reduce the risk and adds blood glucose checks in type 2 diabetes (section 5.4).
Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, etc.)

Using liraglutide with a sulfonylurea may raise the risk of hypoglycemia, including severe hypoglycemia. The Victoza label says to consider a lower sulfonylurea dose when starting liraglutide (section 7.2). Saxenda says a lower dose may reduce the risk (section 5.4).
Digoxin
Liraglutide reduces digoxin AUC by ~16% and Cmax by ~31% via delayed gastric emptying. Monitor digoxin levels if co-administering.

Compounded liraglutide (503A pharmacies): ~$150–$249/month. Liraglutide remains on FDA's drug shortage list as of October 2026. PCAB-accredited 503A pharmacies and telehealth providers offer prescription access. Quality varies by pharmacy; a COA documents each batch.

Liraglutide carries a black box warning for medullary thyroid carcinoma. In rodent studies, liraglutide caused dose-dependent thyroid C-cell tumors at exposures 8 times the human dose. No confirmed human cases appeared in the LEADER trial (0 MTC in the liraglutide arm versus 1 in placebo, n=9,340). Still, the warning makes liraglutide off-limits for anyone with a personal or family history of MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN2). GI side effects are the most common reason people quit. Nausea hits roughly 40% of users at the 3 mg dose. Vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation affect 15 to 20%. The pattern is predictable: symptoms peak during each dose increase and fade over 2 to 3 weeks at a stable dose. Slow titration (advancing by 0.6 mg per week as labeled) reduces the severity. Some community users extend to 2 weeks per step if nausea is severe. Pancreatitis occurs in under 0.4% of patients. The LEADER trial found rates similar to placebo, but the risk is real. Severe abdominal pain radiating to the back, with or without vomiting, means stop the drug and get evaluated immediately. Gallbladder disease showed up in about 2.2% of SCALE trial participants. GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gallbladder emptying, and rapid weight loss adds to gallstone risk. Right upper quadrant pain warrants an ultrasound. LEADER turned up a slight numerical imbalance in total malignancies (10.1% liraglutide versus 9.0% placebo, HR approximately 1.06). This was not statistically significant. The clinical meaning is unclear, but it was observed and should be noted. Hypoglycemia is rare when liraglutide is used alone. It becomes a genuine risk when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas; dose reductions of those medications are often needed. Injection site reactions are mild and infrequent. Hair thinning (telogen effluvium) shows up in community reports. This is driven by rapid weight loss rather than a direct drug effect. It's typically self-limiting. When to seek medical attention: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, signs of allergic reaction, or any visual changes. Stop liraglutide at least 2 months before planned conception; the drug was detected in milk of lactating rats, and human data on infant risk are insufficient.
Common Issues & Solutions

Nausea peaks at each dose increase: if severe, hold current dose for 2 extra weeks before advancing rather than stopping. Ginger tea, small bland meals, and morning dosing (after breakfast) help most users.
If you miss more than 3 consecutive days, restart titration at 0.6 mg: jumping back to your prior dose after a gap causes disproportionate GI side effects.
Constipation at maintenance dose (3 mg) is common: increase fluid intake to ≥2.5L/day, add 25–35 g dietary fiber, consider osmotic laxative (MiraLax) if persistent.

Injection site lumps or reactions: rotate sites each injection: abdomen, thigh, upper arm. Avoid the same spot for at least 1 week. Brand Saxenda pen is a large 32-gauge needle; room-temperature pen reduces injection discomfort.

Weight plateau after initial loss: confirm you are at the 3.0 mg dose. If already at 3 mg and plateaued, review caloric intake: liraglutide suppresses appetite but does not override a significant caloric surplus. Consider switching to semaglutide or tirzepatide for additional efficacy.

Liraglutide holds two active FDA approvals: Victoza (approved 2010) for type 2 diabetes at doses up to 1.8 mg daily, and Saxenda (approved 2014) for chronic weight management at 3.0 mg daily. Both are prescription-only medications. FDA approved the first generic of Victoza (Hikma) in December 2024. Teva's generic of Saxenda followed in August 2025. FDA rates both as therapeutically equivalent to their brands. FDA approved two more Saxenda generics on February 24, 2026, from Biocon (ANDA 217063) and Orbicular (ANDA 217234). Drugs@FDA lists 11 approved liraglutide generics as of October 14, 2026: 8 rated equivalent to Victoza, 3 to Saxenda. Compounded liraglutide is available from 503A pharmacies while liraglutide remains on the FDA drug shortage list. FDA's shortage data still listed it as current in October 2026. PCAB-accredited compounding pharmacies offer prescription access. A Certificate of Analysis (COA) documents potency and purity for each compounded batch. Liraglutide does not appear on the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) 2026 Prohibited List. Among GLP-1 drugs, WADA's 2026 Monitoring Program names only semaglutide and tirzepatide. Athletes subject to anti-doping testing should verify current prohibited substance lists. This content is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting any peptide therapy.

faqs.q: What is the recommended liraglutide dosage for weight loss?
faqs.a: The Saxenda label starts at 0.6 mg daily subcutaneous for one week, then titrates by 0.6 mg each week until reaching 3.0 mg daily. For diabetes (Victoza), the max dose is 1.8 mg daily. Skipping titration steps significantly increases nausea and vomiting rates.

faqs.q: How does liraglutide compare to semaglutide?
faqs.a: Both are GLP-1 agonists from Novo Nordisk. In STEP 8 (PMC8753508), semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly produced 15.8% weight loss versus 6.4% for liraglutide 3 mg daily at 68 weeks. Liraglutide requires daily injections; semaglutide is once weekly. Liraglutide does hold a pediatric approval for ages 12+, which semaglutide does not.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of liraglutide?
faqs.a: Nausea (39%), diarrhea (21%), constipation (19%), and vomiting (16%) per the SCALE trials. GI side effects peak during the first 4-8 weeks of titration. The FDA black box warning covers medullary thyroid carcinoma risk from rodent studies. Pancreatitis, gallbladder events, and acute kidney injury are rare but documented risks.

Yes. Victoza (liraglutide 1.8 mg) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes (2010). Saxenda (liraglutide 3.0 mg) is FDA-approved for chronic weight management (2014). The LEADER trial (n=9,340) also established cardiovascular benefit, leading to a CV risk reduction indication.

faqs.q: How long does liraglutide take to work?
faqs.a: Appetite reduction begins within the first week at the 0.6 mg starting dose. Weight loss becomes measurable by weeks 4-8 as the dose titrates up. The SCALE Obesity trial showed 8% mean weight loss at 56 weeks. Maximum effect requires reaching and maintaining the 3.0 mg daily dose.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of Liraglutide?
faqs.a: The half-life of Liraglutide is ~13 hours. This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: Over 9,300 patients in the LEADER trial. A 13% drop in major cardiovascular events. Liraglutide (Victoza, Saxenda) is a GLP-1 receptor agonist with two FDA approvals and more than 15 years of real-world safety data. The SCALE trial landed on 8% mean weight loss at 56 weeks with the 3 mg dose.
